name: Practitioner glossary
description: Named concepts and trade-offs across enterprise architecture, platform engineering, DevSecOps, SRE, data and applied GenAI.

terms.definition: A short, dated document that captures one architectural decision: context, options, decision and consequences. ADRs are the unit of truth for design history — better than slide decks because they survive leadership change and can be searched, linked and refuted.

An LLM-driven process that plans, calls tools, observes results and iterates toward a goal. Distinct from a single LLM call by its loop and its ability to use external systems. Evaluate agents on cost-per-resolved-task and trajectory quality, not just final output.

Applying machine-learning and pattern-recognition techniques to IT operations data — anomaly detection, alert correlation, root-cause hints. Useful as a layer on top of strong observability; useless as a substitute for it.

A boundary translation layer that prevents the model of one bounded context from leaking into another. The mechanism that lets you incrementally replace a legacy system without inheriting its data model.

A formal authorisation from an accreditation body that a system may operate in a given environment, granted on review of its security controls and risk posture. The artefact that DevSecOps tooling produces continuously, rather than at the end of a release cycle.

A reference framework for banking capability decomposition. A BIAN-aligned target state speeds vendor selection and partner integration — fewer arguments about what a 'customer onboarding' service actually does.
The scope of impact when a component fails. A first-class architectural constraint, not an afterthought. 'How does this fail?' should be a design-review question for every new service.

An incident review that focuses on the systemic conditions that allowed failure, not the individuals who acted within them. The mechanism that turns incidents into platform changes instead of resignations.

Partitioning a system into independent, isolated cells (per region, tenant or shard) so that failure or compromise in one cell doesn't cascade. The pattern that underwrites high availability at scale.

Deliberately injecting failure into systems to verify they degrade safely. Mature chaos engineering is continuous in pre-prod and planned in prod; it is a property of how you build, not an annual exercise.
The amount a team must hold in its head to deliver. Platform engineering's central job is reducing the cognitive load on stream-aligned teams by encoding patterns and providing self-service.
The percentage of steady-state cloud usage covered by reservations or savings plans. Coverage in the 70–90% range typically buys 15–30% before any architectural change.
A hierarchical map of what an organisation does, decoupled from how it does it. A living capability model is the substrate for investment decisions, architecture roadmaps and vendor selection.

Security testing of a running application by sending crafted requests, complementing static (SAST) analysis. Critical findings block merge in mature pipelines; informational findings inform the backlog.
Treating SIEM detections like software: versioned, peer-reviewed, tested against known-good and known-bad signals, deployed through CI. The reason detection coverage stops being a guess.

A container image containing only the application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager. Reduces attack surface and CVE noise; harder to debug but right for most production workloads.
Breaking a monolith along bounded-context lines so each new service owns a coherent slice of the business. Done well, services align with team ownership and have clear, stable contracts.

A test of an LLM's behaviour on a curated set of inputs with known-good outputs. The gate that makes prompt and model changes safe to ship. Evals run continuously in mature programmes, not just before release.
Data leaving a cloud region or account. The mystery line item on cloud bills; the architecture-level driver of cost where caching and co-location pay back fastest.

The allowable amount of unreliability over a time window, derived from an SLO. When the budget is burnt, feature work pauses and reliability work prioritises. Real error budgets change team behaviour; aspirational ones do not.

A style where services communicate by publishing and consuming events rather than calling each other synchronously. Loosens coupling at the cost of observability discipline — distributed traces and a schema registry are non-negotiable.

A switch that decouples deploy from release. Reduces deployment risk (rollback is a flag flip) and enables progressive delivery, A/B testing and per-tenant configuration. Necessary for trunk-based development at scale.
The discipline of making cloud cost a shared engineering, finance and product concern. Mature FinOps shows engineers their cost daily and makes the cheap choice the default choice.

A documented, supported, default way for engineers to ship a common service archetype — pipeline, observability, security baked in. The opposite of a golden cage: teams choose to use it because it's faster than rolling their own.
The four metrics Google recommends every service expose: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. The minimum viable observability for any production service.

An input or output check that prevents an LLM from producing unsafe or off-policy content. Mature guardrails are layered (input policy, model policy, output policy) and tested adversarially, not just trusted because they exist.
The decision rights, controls and audit evidence around how AI systems are built, deployed and used. Risk-tiered governance scales; blanket review committees do not.
Tamper-resistant hardware for cryptographic key storage and operations. The substrate underneath any non-trivial regulated workload — payment, identity, signing.

The set of self-service capabilities — golden paths, service catalogue, environments, secrets, observability — that an engineering org provides to itself. Built well, it's a property of how you build. Built badly, it's a tool stack with a portal on top.
Declaring infrastructure in versioned, diffable code (Terraform, Pulumi, Bicep). The substrate that makes drift detection, policy-as-code and audited change real.
A property of an operation such that running it twice produces the same result as running it once. The minimum design discipline for any retried call across service boundaries.
Granting privileged access for a bounded window on request, with audit, instead of standing privilege. The mechanism that lets you say 'zero standing access' honestly.
The Core Web Vital that measures when the largest visible element finishes rendering. Under 2.5s on cable is the target; over 4s costs revenue at any meaningful scale.
Using one LLM to evaluate the output of another against a rubric. A scalable evals technique — but only when the judge is calibrated against human ratings and re-checked when models change.
A versioned document describing a model's intended use, performance characteristics, evaluation results and known limitations. Required artefact in a regulator-readable AI programme.

terms.term: MTTR / MTTD — Mean time to recovery / detection
terms.definition: The two operational metrics that matter most after availability: how fast you notice a failure and how fast you recover from it. The numbers that improving observability and runbooks are supposed to move.

Identities used by workloads — service accounts, machine certs, API tokens. NHIs outnumber human identities 10–50× and are the dominant attack vector in modern compromises; managed via workload identity (OIDC), not static secrets.
A general-purpose policy engine for enforcing rules across infrastructure and applications. Common substrate for policy-as-code in Kubernetes, CI pipelines and microservice authz.
The property of a system that lets you ask new questions of it without redeploying. Implies logs, metrics, traces, and the discipline to instrument what matters before you need to.
Synonym for golden path. Used to underline that the path exists because the platform paved it, not because teams stumbled onto it.

Encoding security, compliance and architectural rules as machine-evaluated checks — usually OPA, Kyverno or cloud-native equivalents. The mechanism that makes 'security is encoded' more than rhetoric.
The document produced after an incident, capturing timeline, root causes, and action items. Mature programmes track recurrence rate of past failure modes as a primary KPI.

Verifiable evidence of how an artefact was built — who, when, from which source, with which dependencies. SLSA defines escalating levels of provenance assurance; L3+ is the bar for high-risk services.

Architecture that retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge store and includes them in the prompt, so the model answers from grounded context rather than memory. Quality of retrieval is usually the bottleneck, not quality of generation.
Matching cloud resource size to actual demand. The single highest-leverage cost lever after commitment coverage.
An actionable, tested playbook for responding to a known alert or incident. Living runbooks are linked from alerts, tested in game-days, and deprecated when no longer relevant.

A framework for coordinating agile delivery across many teams and programmes. Useful where it's used honestly; ceremony theatre where it's not. The architecture team's job in SAFe is to keep target-state coherent across PIs.
Security analysis of source code without running it. Catches a class of bugs cheaply in CI; suppression discipline is what separates real SAST from theatre.
A signed, machine-readable list of all components in a built artefact. The substrate for supply-chain vulnerability response, license compliance and incident scoping.
Service Level Objective / Indicator. An SLI is a measurable user-experience signal; an SLO is the target on that signal. The right unit of contract between platform, product and ops.

terms.term: SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artefacts
terms.definition: An escalating framework for build-provenance assurance. L1 is having provenance; L3+ is having tamper-resistant build infrastructure with verified provenance on deploy.

Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing new functionality through a façade and migrating existing functionality piece by piece, until the legacy can be retired. The default pattern for high-risk core modernisation.

A model that distinguishes stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem and platform team types, and the interaction patterns between them. The model that gives platform engineering its operating shape.
A structured exercise to identify what could go wrong with a system, by whom, and what controls are in place. Done early in design, it costs hours; done late, it costs sprints.
Repetitive, automatable operational work that has no enduring value. Healthy SRE programmes track toil as a primary KPI and target <50% of team time.
Working in short-lived branches off a single integration branch, with multiple integrations per day, gated by feature flags. The pre-requisite for genuine continuous delivery.
A database optimised for similarity search over high-dimensional embeddings. The retrieval substrate underneath most RAG systems; hybrid retrieval (semantic + keyword) usually beats pure vector.

Authentication for non-human workloads via short-lived, identity-bound credentials (OIDC, IAM roles) rather than static secrets. The single biggest reduction in attack surface available to most organisations.
An identity model in which no principal has privileged access at rest; all privilege is requested, time-bound, audited and revoked automatically. The end-state JIT access points at.
